chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[FIVE COMPILER TYPE -> DEFINITION PAIRS] 1. One pass compiler -> compiles the process in one pass. 2. Two pass compiler -> compiles in two passes; generates intermediate code. 3. Incremental compiler -> recompiles changed source lines / code; updates object code. 4. Native code compiler -> target platform is the same kind as the host platform. 5. Cross compiler -> target platform differs from the host platform. In the original slide each compiler type in a LEFT rounded box is horizontally paired with its explanation in a RIGHT box. The rows do NOT form a top-to-bottom flow or causal chain.

chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[COMPILER VS INTERPRETER - ROW-ALIGNED COMPARISON] Row 1, handling unit: Compiler: scans and translates whole program. Interpreter: translates one statement at a time. Row 2, intermediate code (as the slide claims): Compiler: generates intermediate code. Interpreter: does not generate intermediate code. Row 3, error reporting (as the slide claims): Compiler: errors reported after whole program checked. Interpreter: error reported per interpreted instruction. Row 4, memory (as the slide claims): Compiler: more.    Interpreter: less. Row 5, examples: Compiler: C compiler. Interpreter: Basic, Python, Ruby. CAUTION: These are course-slide generalizations. Interpreters may internally compile to intermediate code / bytecode, and error-reporting behavior is implementation-dependent.

Then, after the lexeme is recorded as an attribute value of a token returned to the parser, lexemeBegin is set to the character immediately after the lexeme just found. ▪Once the next lexeme is determined, the forward is set to the character at its right CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Two pointers: lexemeBegin marks the start of the current lexeme; forward scans ahead to locate its end.

Original lecture content: SENTINELS ▪Each time we move forward, we must check that we have not moved off one of the buffers. Because if we do, we must reload the other buffer. ▪Thus for each character read, we make two tests: one for the end of buffer and one to determine what character is read. ▪The buffer end test can be combined with the test for the current character if we extend each buffer to hold a sentinel character at the end. ▪Sentinel is the special character that cannot be a part of the source program and the natural choice is eof. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Sentinel marks the end of a buffer half; when encountered, check whether to refill or terminate.

PAGE 19 Original lecture content: ▪Most of the times, the lexical analyzer is not able to detect source-code errors. ▪It usually needs aid of other components to perform error-detection. ▪For example: if the source-code (in C language) HANDLING LEXICAL ERRORS encounters 'fi', the lexical analyzer will not detect it as an error and can't tell whether it is a misspelled keyword or an undeclared literal. ▪Since fi is a valid lexeme for the token id, the lexical analyzer must return the token id to the parser and let some other phases (probably the parser in this case) handle an error due to the transposition of letters. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS

PAGE 6 Original lecture content: INTERACTIONS BETWEEN LEXICAL ANALYZER AND PARSER. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Source program -> Lexical Analyzer --token--> Parser -> semantic analysis. Parser --getNextToken--> Lexical Analyzer. Both Lexical Analyzer and Parser interact with Symbol Table.

PAGE 11 Original lecture content: TERMS IN LEXICAL ANALYSIS Token: A pair consisting of token name and an optional attribute value. Remember the form <token-name, attribute-value> Pattern: An informal description of a form that lexemes of a token may take. For e.g. if token is a keyword , then pattern is just the sequence of characters that form the keyword. Lexeme: It is an actual stream of characters (in the source program) that matches the pattern and is identified by the lexical analyzer as an instance of that token. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS

PAGE 23 Original lecture content: ▪Lexical Analyzer often needs to look one or more characters beyond the next lexeme before we can be sure we have the right lexeme. ▪Since the large source programs consist of a large INPUT BUFFERING number of characters and a huge time is required to process those characters, therefore to reduce this overhead, specialized buffering techniques have been developed. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS

PAGE 30 Original lecture content: TOP-DOWN PARSING Homework: recursive descent and parse tree S → if E then S else S | begin L end | print E L → S ; L | ε E → num = num Task Construct a parse tree for: begin print num = num ; end Identify each use of L → ε. CPT316 · Programming Language Implementation and Paradigms PAGE 31 Original lecture content: LL(1) WORKFLOW PREDICTIVE PARSING One expression grammar, six connected steps, one completed parse. CPT316 · TOPIC 3

chunks.heading: PAGE 9
chunks.content:
PAGE 9
Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING Predictive parsing roadmap STEP 3 OF 6 Compute FIRST + FOLLOW Completed / earlier Current focus Next Check left factoring Compute FIRST + FOLLOW Build LL(1) table FIRST predicts beginnings; FOLLOW predicts what may come next. CPT316 · Programming Language Implementation and Paradigms Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING FIRST sets: what can begin a string? A → abc | def | ghi FIRST(A) = { a, d, g } FIRST(α) includes ε only if α can derive the empty string. CPT316 · Programming Language Implementation and Paradigms Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING Computing FIRST correctly If a is a terminal, FIRST(a) = {a}. If A → ε, include ε in FIRST(A). For A → X₁X₂…Xₖ, collect FIRST(X₁) excluding ε; continue to X₂ only if X₁ is nullable. Include ε only when every symbol of that right-hand side can derive ε. Union the contributions from all productions for A. CPT316 · Programming Language Implementation and Paradigms Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING Practice: FIRST for expression grammar E → TE′ E′ → +TE′ | ε T → FT′ T′ → *FT′ | ε F → (E) | id Begin with F, then T′ and E′, then T and E. CPT316 · Programming Language Implementation and Paradigms Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING Running example - FIRST answer Set Value Why FIRST(F) FIRST(T′) FIRST(T) FIRST(E

PAGE 27 Original lecture content: ▪Size of each buffer is usually N, where N is the size of a disk block. ▪Using one system read command, we can read N INPUT BUFFERING characters into the buffer, rather than using one system call per character. ▪Eof marks the end of source file and is different from any possible character of the source program. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Buffer-pair relationship: two adjacent input buffer halves are used alternately for scanning.

PAGE 32 Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING Predictive parsing is a top-down parsing without backtracking Predictive parsing is also called LL(k) parsing The first L stands for scanning the input from left to right The second L stands for producing a leftmost derivation The k stands for using k lookahead input symbol to choose alternative productions at each derivation step Namely, according to the next token, there is only one production to choose at each derivation step Therefore , it is also know as LL(1) parsing from now on, namely, parsing using only one lookahead input symbol (one token)

PAGE 32 Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING Predictive parsing is a top-down parsing without backtracking Predictive parsing is also called LL(k) parsing The first L stands for scanning the input from left to right The second L stands for producing a leftmost derivation The k stands for using k lookahead input symbol to choose alternative productions at each derivation step Namely, according to the next token, there is only one production to choose at each derivation step Therefore , it is also know as LL(1) parsing from now on, namely, parsing using only one lookahead input symbol (one token)

Original lecture content: Step 1: Elimination of Left Recursion STEPS FOR PREDICTIVE PARSING Step 2: Elimination of Left Factor Grammar Step 3: Find First & Follow Step 4: Construct Parsing Table Step 5 : Parsing input string Step 6 : Construct the parse tree PAGE 45 Original lecture content: LEFT-FACTORING Left factoring is a process by which the grammar with common prefixes is transformed to make it useful for Top down parsers. Example A → ab | ac This kind of grammar creates a problematic situation for Top down parsers. Top down parsers can not decide which production must be chosen to parse the string since two or more rules start with the same beginning To remove this confusion, we use left factoring.

generation.answer:
The source code first yields identifiers that the scanner turns into tokens, which the parser arranges into a parse tree. In the example the tree initially has the literal 60 as an integer leaf under the multiplication node. During semantic analysis a conversion node (inttoreal) is inserted above that literal so the integer is coerced to a real before the multiplication, producing a tree that now includes the type‑conversion step.

- **Scanning**: identifiers become tokens that feed the parser [3]
- **Parsing**: the initial parse tree shows the assignment, addition, multiplication and the integer literal 60 [2]
- **Semantic analysis**: inserts an inttoreal conversion node above 60 to change its type from integer to real before multiplication [2]

CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Compiler pipeline: Source language -> Scanner (lexical analysis) -> tokens -> Parser (syntax analysis) -> syntax tree -> Semantic Analysis / IC generator -> intermediate language -> Code Optimizer -> Code Generator -> target language. Original lecture content: Symbols: +, -, *, /, =, <, >, ->, … Keywords: if, while, struct, float, int, … TYPICAL TOKENS IN Integer and Real (floating point) literals 123, 123.45 A PL Char (string) literals Identifiers Comments White space CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS

PAGE 19 Original lecture content: ▪Most of the times, the lexical analyzer is not able to detect source-code errors. ▪It usually needs aid of other components to perform error-detection. ▪For example: if the source-code (in C language) HANDLING LEXICAL ERRORS encounters 'fi', the lexical analyzer will not detect it as an error and can't tell whether it is a misspelled keyword or an undeclared literal. ▪Since fi is a valid lexeme for the token id, the lexical analyzer must return the token id to the parser and let some other phases (probably the parser in this case) handle an error due to the transposition of letters. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS

Original lecture content: SINGLE VS TWO-BUFFER Single Buffering Double Buffering/ Two- Buffer ▪The compiler loads a substantial segment of ▪The lexical analyzer processes characters the source file into a buffer. from one buffer ▪The lexical analyzer processes the buffer ▪The second buffer is simultaneously loaded character by character to detect tokens. with the next set of characters from the source file. ▪Once the buffer is depleted, it is refilled with the next set of characters, and the cycle continues. ▪This concurrent processing and reading ensure a steady stream of characters and minimizes wait times. ▪This approach can be inefficient as it requires processing to halt each time the buffer is replenished. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Input buffering comparison: single buffer versus two-buffer arrangement. Buffer use is related to repeated character reads during lexical scanning.

generation.answer:
A two‑pass structure solves forward references by separating analysis and code generation into two scans. In the first pass the source program is read and information such as declarations, symbols, and addresses is recorded. In the second pass the recorded information is used together with the source program to generate the target code, so definitions that appear later are already known when needed.

- **First pass**: analyzes the program and records relevant information like symbols and addresses. [2]
- **Second pass**: uses the recorded information to generate the final code, allowing earlier uses of identifiers to be resolved after their definitions are seen. [2]

chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[FRONT END VS BACK END - GROUPING] FRONT END (primarily source-language-dependent): - Lexical analysis - Syntax analysis - Semantic analysis - Intermediate code generation - Creation of symbol table BACK END (primarily target-machine-dependent): - Code optimization - Code generation phase - Error handling and symbol table operation These are two GROUPS of compiler work, not two data entities. The grouping is as stated by the lecture; actual compiler implementations may move some services between front and back.

chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[COMPILER VS INTERPRETER - ROW-ALIGNED COMPARISON] Row 1, handling unit: Compiler: scans and translates whole program. Interpreter: translates one statement at a time. Row 2, intermediate code (as the slide claims): Compiler: generates intermediate code. Interpreter: does not generate intermediate code. Row 3, error reporting (as the slide claims): Compiler: errors reported after whole program checked. Interpreter: error reported per interpreted instruction. Row 4, memory (as the slide claims): Compiler: more.    Interpreter: less. Row 5, examples: Compiler: C compiler. Interpreter: Basic, Python, Ruby. CAUTION: These are course-slide generalizations. Interpreters may internally compile to intermediate code / bytecode, and error-reporting behavior is implementation-dependent.

chunks.content: Original lecture content: STEPS FOR PREDICTIVE PARSING (STEP 4) Algorithm to construct LL(1) Parsing Table For each production A -> α. 1. Find First(α) and for each terminal in First(α), make entry A -> α in the table. 2. If First(α) contains ε (epsilon) as terminal, then find the Follow(A) and for each terminal in Follow(A), make entry A -> ε in the table. 3. If the First(α) contains ε and Follow(A) contains $ as terminal, then make entry A -> ε in the table for the $.

Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING Running example - FOLLOW answer Set Value Main source FOLLOW(E) FOLLOW(E′) FOLLOW(T) FOLLOW(T′) FOLLOW(F) FOLLOW sets accumulate from every relevant occurrence and never contain ε. CPT316 · Programming Language Implementation and Paradigms PAGE 62 Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING Predictive parsing roadmap STEP 4 OF 6 Build LL(1) table Completed / earlier Current focus Next Compute FIRST + FOLLOW Build LL(1) table Parse input with stack Use FIRST and FOLLOW to place each production in a table. CPT316 · Programming Language Implementation and Paradigms PAGE 63 Original lecture content: PREDICTIVE PARSING Correct algorithm: construct the LL(1) table For each production A → α: For every terminal a in FIRST(α) - {ε}, enter A → α in M[A, a]. If ε is in FIRST(α), enter A → α in M[A, b] for every b in FOLLOW(A). Unused cells indicate syntax errors. If any cell needs two different productions, the grammar is not LL(1). Important: write the actual production A → α, not automatically A → ε. CPT316 · Programming Language Implementation and Paradigms Diagram representation / semantic relationships: For each production A -> alpha: for terminals a in FIRST(alpha), add A -> alpha to M[A,a]; if epsilon in FIRST(alpha), add it to M[A,b] for b in FOLLOW(A). Conflicting entries imply non-LL(1).

PAGE 55 Original lecture content: EXAMPLE - COMPUTING FOLLOW The following grammar has been eliminated for left recursion and left factor grammar. E→TE' E' →+TE' | T →FT' T' →*FT' | F →( E) | id Original lecture content: Step 1: Elimination of Left Recursion STEPS FOR PREDICTIVE PARSING Step 2: Elimination of Left Factor Grammar Step 3: Find First & Follow Step 4: Construct Parsing Table Step 5 : Parsing input string Step 6 : Construct the parse tree PAGE 57 Original lecture content: The first 'L' in LL(1) stands for scanning the input from left to right, The second "L' for producing a leftmost derivation The '1' for using one input symbol of look ahead at each step to make parsing action decisions. LL (1) PARSING TABLE Before LL(1) generates the parse tree, LL(1) parsing table need to be produced first PAGE 58 Original lecture content: MODEL OF LL(1) PARSER A predictive parser has: Stack - a sequence of grammar symbols with $ on the bottom, indicating the bottom of the stack. Initially the stack consists of the start symbol of the grammar on the top of $. Input - the string to be parsed, followed by $, a symbol used as a right end marker to indicate the end of the input string Parsing Table Output Diagram representation / semantic relationships: LL(1) parser has an input buffer, stack, parsing table, and output actions. The top-of-stack nonterminal and current lookahead token determine the production.

generation.answer:
A compiler reads the whole program, scans it and translates the entire source into an intermediate form or target code before any execution, while an interpreter processes the source line‑by‑line, translating and executing each statement one at a time.

- **Compiler**: scans the whole program, generates intermediate code, and reports errors only after the entire program has been checked. It typically uses more memory because it holds the whole translation in advance. Examples include C compilers. [1]
- **Interpreter**: translates one statement at a time ("line by line"), does not produce a separate intermediate or binary file, and reports errors as each instruction is interpreted. It generally uses less memory. Examples include Basic, Python, Ruby. [1] [2]

Loader relocates addresses and places instructions/data at appropriate memory locations.

generation.answer:
The **linker** takes the separate relocatable object files (and any libraries) that were produced by the compiler/assembler and merges them into a single program image. The **loader** then takes that linked program, adjusts the address references so they point to the actual memory locations where the code and data will reside, and places the instructions and data into those locations in memory.

- **Linker**: combines code from several relocatable object files and libraries into one program. [1]
- **Loader**: relocates addresses and places instructions/data at appropriate memory locations. [1]

questions.author: original
questions.reference_answer: A forward reference is a use that appears before its later definition, so a one-pass compiler may not know the definition yet when generating code. A two-pass compiler fixes this by recording declarations/symbols/addresses in pass 1 and generating target code in pass 2.
required_facts: Forward reference is a use before a later definition
One-pass code generation is hard because the definition may not be known yet
Pass 1 records relevant information (declarations, symbols, addresses)
Pass 2 generates target code using the recorded information

alternatives.quote: A forward reference means a use appears BEFORE a later definition in the source order.
A forward reference can make immediate one-pass code generation difficult, because a referenced definition may not be known yet.
Source program -> analyze -> record relevant information
Source program + recorded information -> generate target code

Original lecture content: SINGLE VS TWO-BUFFER Single Buffering Double Buffering/ Two- Buffer ▪The compiler loads a substantial segment of ▪The lexical analyzer processes characters the source file into a buffer. from one buffer ▪The lexical analyzer processes the buffer ▪The second buffer is simultaneously loaded character by character to detect tokens. with the next set of characters from the source file. ▪Once the buffer is depleted, it is refilled with the next set of characters, and the cycle continues. ▪This concurrent processing and reading ensure a steady stream of characters and minimizes wait times. ▪This approach can be inefficient as it requires processing to halt each time the buffer is replenished. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Input buffering comparison: single buffer versus two-buffer arrangement. Buffer use is related to repeated character reads during lexical scanning.

Original lecture content: SENTINELS ▪Each time we move forward, we must check that we have not moved off one of the buffers. Because if we do, we must reload the other buffer. ▪Thus for each character read, we make two tests: one for the end of buffer and one to determine what character is read. ▪The buffer end test can be combined with the test for the current character if we extend each buffer to hold a sentinel character at the end. ▪Sentinel is the special character that cannot be a part of the source program and the natural choice is eof. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Sentinel marks the end of a buffer half; when encountered, check whether to refill or terminate.

generation.answer: A forward reference occurs when a program uses a name before its definition appears in the source order [1]. In a single‑pass compiler the code for a statement must be generated as soon as the statement is read, so if the statement refers to something that has not been defined yet, the compiler has no information about its address or type and cannot emit correct target code [2]. The two‑pass solution solves this by separating analysis from code generation: Pass I scans the whole source, records all declarations and other needed information, and Pass II scans again, now equipped with the complete symbol table, to generate the final code [1].

generation.answer: The compiler does not jump straight from analysis to generating the target program because it needs a **middle representation** – the Intermediate Representation (IR) – to act as a bridge between the two big groups of work.  During the **analysis phase** the source code is broken down, its tokens are identified, its syntax is checked and its meaning is understood; all of this information is collected into the IR [1] "Output of analysis = Intermediate Representation".  Then the **synthesis phase** can take that structured, language‑independent description and apply optimisations and code‑generation steps to produce the final binary [1] "Input to synthesis = Intermediate Representation".  In other words, the IR lets the compiler separate the concerns of *understanding* the program from *producing* the executable, making each phase simpler and allowing the same IR to be reused for different target machines or optimisation passes [2] "The intermediate representation is a bridge: analysis extracts/structures meaning; synthesis constructs output".

Original lecture content: SENTINELS ▪Each time we move forward, we must check that we have not moved off one of the buffers. Because if we do, we must reload the other buffer. ▪Thus for each character read, we make two tests: one for the end of buffer and one to determine what character is read. ▪The buffer end test can be combined with the test for the current character if we extend each buffer to hold a sentinel character at the end. ▪Sentinel is the special character that cannot be a part of the source program and the natural choice is eof. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Sentinel marks the end of a buffer half; when encountered, check whether to refill or terminate.

PAGE 60 Original lecture content: TRANSITION DIAGRAMS Consists of: 1. A collection of nodes or circles, called states. Each state represents a condition that could occur during the process of scanning the input looking for a lexeme that matches one of several patterns 2. Edges are directed from one state of the transition diagram to another. Each edge is labeled by a symbol or set of symbols. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Transition diagrams represent lexical recognition as directed states and input-labeled transitions. Acceptance is indicated by designated final states.

PAGE 31 Original lecture content: SENTINELS ▪Note that eof retains its use as a marker for the end of entire input. ▪Any eof that appears other than at the end of buffer means that the input is at an end. CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: EOF sentinel can represent an end-of-buffer boundary or true end-of-input depending on buffer position and refill result.

chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[PASS STRUCTURE / TEMPORAL ORDER] Definition: a "pass" is one complete scan through the program. ONE-PASS structure: read/analyze source statement -> synthesize corresponding output (for each statement in the same pass) TWO-PASS structure: Pass 1: analysis -> intermediate information Pass 2: use intermediate information -> target output A forward reference can make immediate one-pass code generation difficult, because a referenced definition may not be known yet.

chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[TWO-PASS SOLUTION TO FORWARD REFERENCES] A forward reference means a use appears BEFORE a later definition in the source order. Pass I (first scan): Source program -> analyze -> record relevant information (e.g., declarations, symbols, addresses) Pass II (second scan): Source program + recorded information -> generate target code The two horizontal bars "Pass I" and "Pass II" introduce SEPARATE operations; they are not branches run in parallel.

chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[FIVE COMPILER TYPE -> DEFINITION PAIRS] 1. One pass compiler -> compiles the process in one pass. 2. Two pass compiler -> compiles in two passes; generates intermediate code. 3. Incremental compiler -> recompiles changed source lines / code; updates object code. 4. Native code compiler -> target platform is the same kind as the host platform. 5. Cross compiler -> target platform differs from the host platform. In the original slide each compiler type in a LEFT rounded box is horizontally paired with its explanation in a RIGHT box. The rows do NOT form a top-to-bottom flow or causal chain.

generation.answer: Using fewer passes can reduce the amount of reading and writing of intermediate files, which sounds attractive, but the downside is that it often requires the compiler to keep more information in memory because several phases are combined into one pass[1]. Moreover, certain language features such as forward references—where a use appears before its definition—make single‑pass code generation difficult, because the needed definition may not be known yet; a two‑pass approach solves this by first collecting declarations and then generating code in a second scan[2] [3].

generation.answer: LR parsing is a bottom‑up technique that builds a parse by repeatedly **shifting** input tokens onto a stack and then **reducing** sequences of symbols that match the right‑hand side of a grammar rule back to the rule’s left‑hand side.  A shift action moves the next token from the input onto the parsing stack, while a reduce action replaces a recognized handle (a substring that forms the right‑hand side of a production) with the corresponding non‑terminal symbol, effectively constructing the parse tree from the leaves toward the start symbol.  LR parsers belong to the bottom‑up LR family, which use shift‑reduce operations to recognize a wider range of deterministic context‑free grammars than top‑down LL parsers and reconstruct a rightmost derivation in reverse.[2] [5]

chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[FRONT END VS BACK END - GROUPING] FRONT END (primarily source-language-dependent): - Lexical analysis - Syntax analysis - Semantic analysis - Intermediate code generation - Creation of symbol table BACK END (primarily target-machine-dependent): - Code optimization - Code generation phase - Error handling and symbol table operation These are two GROUPS of compiler work, not two data entities. The grouping is as stated by the lecture; actual compiler implementations may move some services between front and back.

chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[COMPILER PHASE HIERARCHY - FOCUS CHANGE] Same directed phase graph as slide 12. Pink highlighted node: Intermediate code generation. Location: after semantic analysis and before code optimization. The text label "Intermediate code generation" names the bridge between the analysis and synthesis groups in this slide's model.

chunks.heading: Token classes:
chunks.content:
Token classes:
[COMPILER VS INTERPRETER - ROW-ALIGNED COMPARISON] Row 1, handling unit: Compiler: scans and translates whole program. Interpreter: translates one statement at a time. Row 2, intermediate code (as the slide claims): Compiler: generates intermediate code. Interpreter: does not generate intermediate code. Row 3, error reporting (as the slide claims): Compiler: errors reported after whole program checked. Interpreter: error reported per interpreted instruction. Row 4, memory (as the slide claims): Compiler: more.    Interpreter: less. Row 5, examples: Compiler: C compiler. Interpreter: Basic, Python, Ruby. CAUTION: These are course-slide generalizations. Interpreters may internally compile to intermediate code / bytecode, and error-reporting behavior is implementation-dependent.

PAGE 3 Original lecture content: REMEMBER? CPT316 PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATION AND PARADIGMS Diagram representation / semantic relationships: Compiler pipeline: Source language -> Scanner (lexical analysis) -> tokens -> Parser (syntax analysis) -> syntax tree -> Semantic Analysis / IC generator -> intermediate language -> Code Optimizer -> Code Generator -> target language. Symbol Table has cross-stage connections to scanner, parser, semantic analysis, optimizer and code generator.
